### Post-QC-workshop consulation (17/8/26)

Sara:

Hi Rahma,

Thanks for joining me over Zoom. I’m sending you a short recap on what we discussed just now.

**Display settings**

If you’re not interested in running quantitative analysis on your images, and showing some images for qualitative comparison instead, you can adjust the display settings (Brightness and Contrast in Fiji), and save the resulting image as PNG files.

- I’d recommend PNG over jpeg as it uses `lossless`​ compression and hence preserves details better. 
- It’s best to keep your display settings consistent across the conditions you’re comparing (i.e., across developmental timepoints).
  - No need to maintain the settings for different probes.
- Inside Fiji’s _Brightness and Contrast_ window you can go to “Set” to see what Minimum and Maximum values you have.
  - You also have a checkbox (“Propagate to all other open images") that applies the same settings to all the images you currently have open – a big time saver!
- Decide on display parameters by using a few images that visible look different, and then apply it to the rest of them. This is just in case the settings that work great for one image, don’t work well for others.

**Making a sub-stack** 

If you’re only interested in the middle slices of your sample, you can make a sub-stack of your image before you generate the Maximum Intensity Projection (i.e., Z-projection).

- _Image > Duplicate_. You can then input the slices you want to keep in the “Range” section.

**Histograms**

To get a clearer idea on what the signal is like, you can open the image histogram by going to _Analyze > Histogram_. That gives you a bigger histogram with detailed information on your intensity (such as the mean value or standard deviation). It could be a nice addition to your presentation.

**Controls** (for the future)

Determining why you have low signal in any of your probes is quite challenging if you don’t know what to expect. That’s why it’s very valuable to have negative and positive controls, where you know you should expect an increase/decrease in signal, as a sanity check. Right now, low signal could be explained by issues with your sample prep/acquisition. A valuable piece of information to add to your presentation and final project.

**Community-developed checklist for image publication**

There’s a very useful checklist for publishing microscopy images (and analyses) in [this](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41592-023-01987-9 "‌")Nature article. I’d recommend you have a look at it. A few points might be overkill for an internal presentation rather than a paper, but it’s a great reference point when you’re handling images. 

‌

Feel free to get in touch if you have any further questions.

Best of luck!

Sara

**Machine learning-based image analysis with Ilastik (28/08)**

Dear all,

Thanks for signing up for the "Machine learning-based image analysis with Ilastik<https://intranet.crick.ac.uk/seminar/image-analysis-machine-learning-based-image-analysis-ilastik-2026-08-28t080000>" workshop, taking place in Training Room 1 on the first floor on Friday 28th August. 

You can find the full program on the event page. We start at 9 am, coffee and tea will be available on arrival. 

In preparation of the workshop, you'll need to do the following: 

  *
Download the latest Stable version of Fiji following this link<https://imagej.net/software/fiji/downloads>. If you already have Fiji on your laptop, update your current installation by going to the Help> Update menu   *
Download ilastik on your laptop following the instructions here<https://www.ilastik.org/documentation/basics/installation>   *
Download the sample data, which you can find at this link<https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/1uqNnM0ioKmF0GA81oIeUReyOD0mvVoYH?usp=sharing>. Please save this folder somewhere in your computer with no spaces or special characters in the file path (e.g., /Stefania/Downloads/) 

You will need to bring your laptop and charger. A computer mouse will also be helpful to interact with ilastik. 

If you are no longer planning to attend, please cancel your spot on Workday, so that we can offer your place to someone else. 

Let us know should you have any questions!

Best wishes,
Stefania

Stefania Marcotti

BioImage Analysis Trainer
Crick Image Analysis Group
Crick Advanced Light Microscopy (CALM) STP
The Francis Crick Institute
London, UK

Hi Maria,

Thanks for your time earlier! Below is a recap of what we've discussed. Please get in touch should you have any questions or require further assistance. 

Best wishes,
Stefania

---

  *
It's good practice to open images in Fiji using Bio-Formats<https://www.openmicroscopy.org/bio-formats/> to make sure that metadata is read correctly and that all Series in a file are taken into account. You can do so by using File> Import> Bio-Formats.   *
It might be good to check a few of the images in your dataset to make sure the signal-to-noise ratio is good enough for analysis. It might be that some staining in some conditions hasn't quite worked as expected; we can still quantify these channels, but the results might not be very meaningful!   *
You can look at the histograms for each channel using the Analyse> Histogram menu. Histograms are a representation of the signal in an image: this can go from 0 (black) to 2^bit-depth (white). The images have been acquired at 16-bit, so you can get to a maximum value of 65535. If foreground and background have very similar intensity values, it means the signal-to-noise ratio isn't very good, and quantification might be challenging.   *
To quantify expression in different channels, we first need to define regions of interest. This can be done by segmenting the DAPI channel. The easiest way to perform segmentation is thresholding<https://neubias.github.io/training-resources/binarization/index.html>, which works by splitting the histogram in two parts using one of the default algorithms (Image> Adjust> Threshold). The result of segmentation is a binary mask, which only takes two values, either 0 (background) or 255 (foreground).   *
We then need to assign a unique ID to each object. We can do so by using a plugin called MorphoLibJ<https://imagej.net/plugins/morpholibj> (MLJ), which implements an algorithm called connected components labelling<https://neubias.github.io/training-resources/connected_components/index.html> (Plugins> MLJ> Binary masks> Connected component labelling). The result is a label mask, which is 0 on the background and assigns an integer ID to each object. Each object can now be queried separately, to investigate both its morphological features and signal intensity. Label masks can be filtered (e.g., by object area) to only analyse a subset of the data (Plugins> MLJ> Label Images> Label Size Filtering)   *
Still using MorphoLibJ, we can obtain a table of object areas (Plugins> MLJ> Analyse> Analyse Regions) and mean signal intensity on any channels of interest (Plugins> MLJ> Analyse> Intensity Measurements 2D/3D). The latter takes two inputs: the label image obtained on the DAPI channel and the raw channel you want to quantify (e.g., green), which needs to be split into its own separate window (Image> Colour> Split Channel or Image> Duplicate).   *
The output of the analysis is a table, which can be saved as a CSV and opened in Excel or other software. The first step would be to plot the distributions of mean intensities across different samples to check for obvious trends. Alternatively, you could set an intensity threshold on each channel to decide whether a cell is positive or negative, and calculate the percentage of positive cells over the total in each image. If you need assistance with statistics or data analysis, I would strongly advise having a chat with the Biostatistics team<https://intranet.crick.ac.uk/our-crick/bioinformatics-biostatistics/pages/statistics>; they offer this service free of charge.   *
You can automate the analysis pipeline using Fiji macros. Here's a tutorial<https://imagej.net/tutorials/batch-processing-with-ij-macro> to get you started.

old.desc:
Dear Adam,


You can copy your image data from 


smb://data2.thecrick.org/proj-omero/karouta/omero_transferred


You can find out a bit more from Crick OMERO Guide
https://franciscrickinstitute.github.io/crick-omeroguide/access.html


With regard to your question, that you have a copy of your images on your laptop
without wifi access, you want to do some analysis, but after you have wifi
access, you  want to continue the work using OMERO via QuPath extension.
We believe that there are 2 possible ways to do that:
 1. In theory you can do your analysis on the images on your laptop. When you
    have access to QuPath extension, you can either rename your folder where the
    images are located, this will trigger QuPath to ask you for the location of
    your files, you should be able to use the QuPath extension to point that to
    your images in OMERO.
 2. The other option is to do your analysis on the images on your laptop, but
    "create the command history script” under Automate on the top menu. After
    you have access to OMERO, you can open those images in OMERO and re-run the
    command script that you have saved.



You may want to explore these 2 options before to test out what work best for
you.


Best regards
Ken

### Connecting to OMERO via Fiji-OnDemand:

Email thread below.

---

Sara:

Hi Lies, 

Now that your data lives in OMERO, you need to download the OMERO plugin in your Fiji OnDemand (instructions [here](https://franciscrickinstitute.github.io/crick-omeroguide/fiji/docs/installation.html#installation-of-the-omero-plugin-for-fiji-and-imagej "‌")). Once you have it downloaded, you go to _Plugins > OMERO > Connect to OMERO._ In the OMERO window that open, put your usual login details and you’ll then have access to all your files in OMERO (which live in _Demo > DEMO CALM_STP_). By clicking on your image of interest, the usual BioFormats importer window will pop up. 

![Screenshot 2026-08-10 at 12.11.01.png](cid:2381619131*ADD0D390-47DF-4461-AEE2-EBE66F97CB12)

I hope that helps! If you run into any issues, just let us know. 

Best wishes, 

Sara

### Initial meeting (11/8/26)

Zoom: Javier, Sara. Recap email:

Hi Javier, 

Thanks for your time today! Here’s a recap of what we’ve discussed, with some useful links to get you started – beware, long email incoming!

————

**QuPath OnDemand**

Now that you have access to [OnDemand](https://ondemand001.nemo.thecrick.org/ "‌"), you can access the pre-installed version of QuPath on the cluster by following[ these instructions](https://franciscrickinstitute.github.io/Image-Analysis-Group/software_instructions/QuPath/ "‌"). 

- You’ll have to go through the terminal every time you want to open QuPath. Alternatively, we can add an icon on your Nemo Desktop if you’d like!

**QuPath workflow**

As we discussed, because it’s your first time using QuPath, start simple. Try getting a workflow to script where you can get the surface of the lung covered by viral stain. Then, we can start extracting more complex measurements. A simple workflow to start with could look like:

1. Import images with OMERO 
2. Estimate the stain vector (instructions [here](https://qupath.readthedocs.io/en/stable/docs/tutorials/separating_stains.html#estimating-stain-vectors "‌")), and use those values for all your images. 
3. Find your tissue of interest using a [threshold](https://qupath.readthedocs.io/en/stable/docs/tutorials/thresholding.html "‌") (_Classify > Pixel classification > Create threshold_). 

- You can _Create objects_ once you’re happy with the result, and split them so each piece of tissue is treated as a separate annotation. 

1. Detect your SCV2-positive areas with either:

      4.1. Threshold

- Start simple. In the same way you create a threshold for the Tissue, you can do the same for your DAB channel.
- Just make sure you run it inside the Tissue regions.
- Try the same threshold on images from different samples, conditions, and batches. If it holds up nicely, you can stick to this method. If the variability throws off the threshold, then try the next method. 

      4.2. [Pixel classifier](https://qupath.readthedocs.io/en/stable/docs/tutorials/pixel_classification.html "‌")

- I’d recommend you create a separate QuPath project folder to train your classifier. It’ll make life a lot easier. Once you’re done,  you just need to copy paste the .json file inside the project folder (located within the `classifiers`​ folder) into the other project folder where you’re running your analysis. 
- Inside this separate folder, you can add different training images. If you add a few positive and negative annotations to images from different samples/conditions/batches, it’ll take into account that variability. 
- Ensure that when you’re training the classifier, you select the button _Load training_. There you can select all the images in the project where you have annotations, instead of just training it with the currently opened image. 
- You can also play around with the _Features_, where you select what information goes into the classifier. There’s more detailed explanations [here](https://qupath.readthedocs.io/en/stable/docs/tutorials/pixel_classification.html#selecting-features "‌"). 

1. Export measurements:

-  Once you’re happy with the parameters from the steps above, try running it on a mini-test-dataset: 3 images (non-infected, mild viral load, and high viral load).
- That should give you an idea on how well the pipeline’s working. 
- You can export the measurements via _Measure > Export measurements_. Ensure you have _Object type_ with “Annotations” selected.
  - Tick “project metadata” too, so you can have columns showing the experimental info that you input.

**Scripting**

Once you are happy with the workflow, try creating a script the way I showed you today. Here are a couple of useful pages to check out that can help you get started:

- QuPath [documentation](https://qupath.readthedocs.io/en/stable/docs/scripting/overview.html "‌")
- ImageScientist’s [useful commands ](https://www.imagescientist.com/useful-simple-commands "‌")

**Follow-up meeting**

Once you’ve done a bit more progress, in your own time, reach out to us again and we can set another follow-up meeting. 

————

If you have any issues/questions/doubts in the meantime, feel free to Slack me or drop us an email again. 

Best of luck!

Sara

Subject: RE: Help with image analysis - YAP N/C measures

Dear Laura,
I assume you also used ImageJ.

The mean intensity is averaged over all the pixels, so unbiased by the cell size and pixel size calibration. The integrated intensity is the sum of all the pixels intensities and will change if your treated cells also show some change in size. 

Also, please check if the image you measure are all calibrated in the same way, since if you consider "IntDen" measurement in ImageJ it changes depending on the pixel size property, while RawIntDen remains constant. 

Perhaps the difference you see is due to this?

A nice post on the forum on the same topic is here:
https://forum.image.sc/t/mean-gray-intensity-integrated-density-and-raw-integrated-density/4983 

Hope it helps.
Best regards,
Rocco

Subject: Help with frequency domain FLIM analysis?

Hi image analysis team,

I think I’ve met most of you already but I’m one of the clinical PhD students in Mike Devine’s lab. I was hoping to get some help with analysis of frequency domain FLIM data - which Matt has been helping me a lot with already. 

I’m using both the Toggel (frequency domain FLIM) and Falcon (TCSPC FLIM) systems to look at inter-organellar contact sites using FRET in both primary neurons and HeLa cells. The Toggel in particular has been a lot of work - and to get useful data out of it what I’ve ended up doing is a slightly complicated workflow which involves maths I don’t fully understand with a large helping hand from Claude - so was hoping to sense check and get help from someone who actually knows what they’re doing! 

The Toggel is a two-chip CMOS camera with a modulated light source. It outputs raw data in .fli files (which can open in BioFormats, and contain a stack of phase-shifted intensity images) which we calibrate to reference dyes with a known lifetime after a Phasor transformation. Because of readout delays on the chip, and the need for quite high sensitivity for quite small areas of FRET, I’ve ended up needing to use multiple references (using fluorescein quenched with varying amounts of potassium iodide and multiple exposures) which I create an intensity weighted scaled rotation matrix from, which I then apply to calibrate the samples' raw transformed s and g values. We capture in MicroManager, so also get .ome.tiff files - Matt’s made a pipeline which I’ve adapted where the raw .fli files are uploaded to Omero and are then used to fit each .ome.tiff image - which is useful because it allows eg timelapses and multi dimensional acquisition. Ultimately, downstream, I want to look at contact persistence and dynamics using mSLIC clustering of Phasor plots, which is hopefully relatively straightforward from these fitted Omero images. 

Overall - I was hoping that someone might be able to help with the maths involved (which I don’t fully understand), help streamline some of the code for eg sharing on Github later (because I’m very much no Python expert) and maybe help with some of the downstream analysis. Currently, there’s no real useful way to examine these contact sites in live cells, so we hope this approach might overcome some limitations in the field and be moderately impactful! 

Thanks very much in advance,

Jonny Spencer

**helpdesk follow-up**

Hi, Risha and Amélie,

Thanks again for stopping by the helpdesk earlier!

Please find below a recap of what we've discussed, with some links which you might find useful. 

The workflow you need to analyse the images should include the following steps: 

  *
Detecting the regions of interest. This would be done by segmenting the puncta on the green channel. Segmentation can be done in different ways; the simplest is thresholding<https://neubias.github.io/training-resources/binarization/index.html>, where we split the histogram into two parts and consider all pixels with a value higher than the threshold as foreground. This results into a binary mask, an image where each pixel can only take one of two values, 0 for background and 1 (or 255 if we're working with 8-bit images) for foreground. In your case, you'll need to filter the detected objects by size, as you're only interested in the larger puncta. This can be done with an algorithm called regionprops, which measures the properties of all detected regions in a binary mask.   *
Measuring the signal of the red channel in the regions of interest. Once we've selected the regions of interest segmenting and filtering the green channel, we can then measure the signal intensity in the red channel for each. The easiest quantification would be the mean grey value per object. Plotting this for ctrl vs treatment should display any difference in "colocalisation" between the two. Please note that, as discussed earlier, this measure alone doesn't tell you whether the two entities interact in any way! Just that they occupy a similar space. 

You can run the analysis in QuPath or Fiji. Below are some instructions for QuPath, let me know if you'd like to switch to Fiji instead. 

  *
The multiplex analysis tutorial<https://qupath.readthedocs.io/en/stable/docs/tutorials/multiplex_analysis.html> should contain all the steps you need. In particular, you'll need to run a Cell Detection<https://qupath.readthedocs.io/en/stable/docs/tutorials/cell_detection.html> using the green channel. You can play around with the parameters to make sure all green puncta are detected (both the non-specific smaller ones and larger ones corresponding to the cells you're interested in). You can keep the "cell expansion" parameter to 0 if you want to solely analyse the nuclei, or add a small region around it as a proxy for the cytoplasm. This operation will automatically measure intensity for both green and red channels and object area. Once you obtain the measurement table<https://qupath.readthedocs.io/en/stable/docs/tutorials/exporting_measurements.html>, you can filter out objects that are too small (non-specific green puncta) and use the mean grey value for the red channel for quantification. 

You can find on this page<https://github.com/FrancisCrickInstitute/Image-Analysis-Group/blob/master/software_instructions/OnDemand/OnDemand.md> the instructions on how to set up image analysis software on OnDemand (HPC wiki here<https://wiki.thecrick.org/display/HPCuserwiki/OnDemand> for OnDemand in general). 

If you need assistance with statistics or data analysis, I would strongly advise having a chat with the Biostatistics team<https://intranet.crick.ac.uk/our-crick/bioinformatics-biostatistics/pages/statistics> in BABS; they offer this service free of charge. 

If you require any further assistance, please get in touch, and we can find a time to have a chat and look at the data in more detail. 

Best wishes,
Stefania

data.text:
Hi Laura,

The mean grey value is the sum of the grey values of all pixels in the region of interest divided by the number of pixels. The integrated density is the sum of the values of the pixels in the region of interest, so it's equivalent to the product of the mean grey value with the area of the region itself. 

In your case, as you're looking at a ratiometric measurement (i.e., nucleus/ cytoplasm), I think it might be better to use the mean grey value, so that the measurement is not affected by the size of the cell. If you imagine two cells with equal mean grey values in both nucleus and cytoplasm, with roughly the same size nuclei, but one with larger cytoplasm, I think one would want for them both to give the same output, as opposed to the larger cell giving a lower ratio. 

Please let me know if this answers your question!

Best wishes,
Stefania

data.text:
**image analysis follow up**

Hi Anastassia!

Please find below a recap of what we've discussed yesterday. If you think I've forgotten anything, or have any further questions, please don't hesitate to get in touch. 

Best wishes,
Stefania

---

  *
Tracking workflow:
     *
Segmentation - this is the process for which we separate the objects of interest from the background. It can be performed by simple histogram thresholding<https://neubias.github.io/training-resources/binarization/index.html> or with more advanced techniques exploiting machine learning. For simple thresholding, setting a threshold with one of the default algorithms in Fiji should do the job (Image> Adjust> Threshold). Make sure to toggle the "Stack histogram" option when working with 3D data. For machine learning methods, you can try ilastik<https://www.ilastik.org/>. They have great online documentation to get you started with a Pixel Classifier workflow<https://www.ilastik.org/documentation/pixelclassification/pixelclassification>. The output of a segmentation step is a binary mask, which will take a value of 0 in the background and 1 (or 255 if the image is 8-bit) in the foreground. All the objects in the image are part of the foreground. Binary masks can be cleaned by morphological filtering<https://neubias.github.io/training-resources/filter_morphological/index.html> or by removing objects with given characteristics (e.g., too large, or too elongated) in Fiji (Process> Binary and Analyse> Analyse Particles).      *
Labelling - the next step involves assigning to each object its own unique ID, to obtain a label mask, where the background takes a value of zero and each object has its own integer ID. To do this, we use an algorithm called connected component labelling<https://neubias.github.io/training-resources/connected_components/index.html>, which you can find in the MorphoLibJ<https://imagej.net/plugins/morpholibj> plugin in Fiji. Label masks can be cleaned by removing objects with given characteristics (e.g., too large, too elongated), still in MorphoLibJ.      *
Tracking - label images can be used as input for TrackMate<https://imagej.net/plugins/trackmate/>. The latest version of TrackMate allows you to use ilastik for segmentation directly within the software, you can read more on their latest publication<https://www.nature.com/articles/s41592-022-01507-1>. Considering that your cells of interest don't seem to be moving too much, you could consider an overlap tracking algorithm, or a more standard LAP option. Both are implemented in TrackMate and described in the paper and documentation. To analyse the results, you can use CellTrackColab<https://github.com/CellMigrationLab/CellTracksColab>, an online tool designed to extract metrics from tracking output files.   *
General considerations:
     *
Open-source - we advise researchers to use open-source software as this improves the reproducibility of workflows. In fact, having access to the source code means that other people can know exactly which steps you took to obtain your results, and can replicate the analysis. You can read more about various considerations on choosing open-source vs. licensed software in this paper<https://doi.org/10.1111%2Fjmi.70109>.      *
Automation - the pipeline described above can be automated in a Fiji macro. Here you can find a tutorial<https://imagej.net/tutorials/batch-processing-with-ij-macro> to get you started.      *
Data analysis - you might want to display your results as 2D plots where one axis represents the starting Z-location of each tracked cell, and the other axis represents one of the metrics obtained for its track in 3D (e.g., distance travelled, persistence, speed). If you need assistance with statistics or data analysis, I would strongly advise having a chat with the Biostatistics team<https://intranet.crick.ac.uk/our-crick/bioinformatics-biostatistics/pages/statistics>; they offer this service free of charge.   *
Working with CALM:
     *
Training workshops - we have a calendar of upcoming workshops<https://intranet.crick.ac.uk/group/514/events> on our webpage, please check each event for more details      *
Training - Get in touch when you have any questions! We'll have a chat similar to the one we had yesterday, in which we can advise on possible next steps and help with troubleshooting. This is currently free of charge      *
Coaching - This is a new format we're testing. The idea is to set a specific timeframe and specific learning goals, which should revolve around learning a methodology rather than performing analysis on a specific dataset. The coaching programme is focused on skills and methods, not research outcomes. To use a paper analogy, we are coaching the Methods section, not the Results. The learning objectives specify the tools that the researcher will be able to use, the techniques they will understand, and the practices they will adopt. While they will be working on data relevant to their research project and receive help in interpreting outputs and troubleshooting the analysis, we can't guarantee that the analytical approaches will ultimately yield the expected biological results. On the other hand, the acquired methodological knowledge should equip the researcher with the relevant skills to tackle not only their current research question, but also to achieve a broader understanding of how to construct workflows for image analysis problems. You would meet regularly with your assigned coach; the sessions are meant for discussion of current progress, not live coding/analysis. CALM staff time would be charged according to current costs<https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1sMPvcBFGiFH3FI68NjZbcOOM439q6NJhBuGYSTCDTVU/edit?usp=sharing>; a cost estimate would be provided upon project agreement, but it's likely going to be around the cost of a medium project.      *
Project work - In this case, CALM staff would prepare the analysis pipeline or analyse a dataset for you. This is the only option in which we would be the ones working on your data directly, but this would still require your input and regular check-ins. CALM staff time would be charged according to current costs; a cost estimate and project plan would be provided upon project agreement.

## 4/8/26 follow-up

Joyce, Katherine Courtis, Stefania, Sara.

Email recap:

Hi Joyce and Katherine, 

Thanks for your time today. It’s great to see the progress you’ve made! As usual, here’s our meeting recap (it’s a particularly long one today).

**Current Fiji analysis**

**Clumped cells**

There are a few things to try to separate your under segmented cells in Fiji:

1. Watershed

- When you have you nuclei binary mask (before you run the _Connected Components Labeling_ command), you can run the watershed algorithm to attempt to split cells based on their morphology.
- _Process > Binary > Watershed_ 

1. Remove big labels

- As you’ve done, you can remove labels that are beyond a specified size in MorphoLibJ.
- You can also extract all the measurements and include a column with ‘Area’ and then remove the rows that correspond to cells beyond a set size.

1. Analyse everything, worry later

- In the whole context of your analysis, the events where you have clumped cells might be insignificant and not worth worrying about.

**Background subtraction**

As Stefania suggested, you might want to subtract the value of the background for each image to your channels of interest, in case it’s affecting the distribution of your GFP/mCherry populations.

- Look at the signal in your labelled mask that corresponds to the background, and use that value to determine a ‘background’ to subtract.
- Note that this might not change much your grouping pattern. We still expect the gradient pattern. 

‌

**Create some “ground truth”** 

Re-calculate manually the counting in a couple of images, and plot this “ground truth” dataset onto your current scatter plot. This will help you decide where to draw the “positivity boundaries”.

      You might end up with 5 groups, depending on how stringent you want to be. But that is an executive decision you’ll have to make once you understand the data a bit better. 

**Check the patterns per image**

You’ve acquired the data on the same sample, with the same imaging settings, at the same time, so it’s unlikely you’ll have significant image-to-image variability. However, you have the analysis script, and it’s worth ruling out this factor. You might see patterns in a single-image basis that you might miss when pooling everything together. 

**Changes in your clustering algorithm**

You could change the number of clusters in your k-mean algorithm, or select a different algorithm that is agnostic to cluster number (e.g., DBSCAN). This is worth exploring once you have your tissue results; it’s not currently very useful. The [Biostatistics](mailto:biostatistics@crick.ac.uk "‌") team are best-suited to advise!

‌

**Tissue analysis**

Start by plotting the exact same graph and clustering analysis with a couple of images from a control and a couple of images from a different condition. The cluster distribution you observe and how it compared to your Fiji-results will inform you on how to continue the project. 

‌

**Intensity value normalisation**

Normalise your intensity values in both your Fiji and QuPath results (e.g., signal goes from 0 to 1), so you can compare both datasets. 

Once you have a better idea on how the data is _behaving_, again, you will have to discuss as a wider group what assumptions and conditions you are working on, and make executive decisions on what to count as positive vs negative. 

‌

**How to work with CALM** (for future reference)
**Coaching**
This is a new format we're testing. The idea is to set a specific timeframe and specific learning goals, which should revolve around learning a methodology more than performing analysis on a specific dataset. The coaching programme is **focused on skills and methods**, not research outcomes. To use a paper analogy, we are coaching the Methods section, not the Results. The learning objectives specify the **tools** that the researcher will be able to use, the techniques they will understand, and the practices they will adopt. While they will be working on data relevant to their research project and receive help in interpreting outputs and troubleshooting the analysis, we can’t guarantee that the analytical approaches will ultimately yield the expected biological results. On the other hand, the acquired methodological knowledge should equip the researcher with the relevant skills to tackle not only their current research question, but also to achieve a broader understanding of how to construct workflows for image analysis problems. You would meet regularly with your assigned coach; the sessions are meant for discussion of current progress, not live coding/analysis. Joint coaching for you and your collaborator could be arranged if of interest. CALM staff time would be charged according to current costs ([CALM Price List](https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1sMPvcBFGiFH3FI68NjZbcOOM439q6NJhBuGYSTCDTVU/edit?usp=sharing "‌"); a cost estimate and coaching plan would be provided upon project agreement).
**Project work**
In this case, CALM staff would prepare the analysis pipeline or analyse a dataset for you. This is the only option in which we would be the ones working on your data directly, but this would still require your input and regular check-ins. CALM staff time would be charged according to current costs; a cost estimate and project plan would be provided upon project agreement.

‌

‌

**MultiDimensional Imaging and Analysis (MDIA) course**

We have one spot left for a Crick researcher to attend our one-week long workshop (14th - 18th September). It’s an intensive course that will teach you how to use several different microscopy systems, when to use which, and different image analysis software. 

There is more information on our IntraNet page [here](https://intranet.crick.ac.uk/seminar/microscopy-multi-dimensional-imaging-and-analysis-training-workshop-2026-09-14t080000 "‌"), in case it is of use to any of your colleagues!

‌

‌

‌

As usual, let us know if you encounter any hurdles or have any questions in the meantime. 

Best wishes, 

Sara

Good morning,

Feedback
We run image analysis workshops regularly, so it would be great if you could fill in this short feedback form<https://forms.cloud.microsoft/e/rqDThtKJJu>, if you haven’t done so already. It’s completely anonymous, and it’s very informative for us to help us improve our training courses. 

Further support
We recently set up UK-BIAS<https://sjcross.github.io/UK-BIAS/>, a distributed node for image analysis support within Euro-Bioimaging<https://www.eurobioimaging.eu/>. We are accepting project requests from researchers who wants support with image analysis. You could access this service free of charge by applying to the Bioimaging-UK User Access funding<https://www.rms.org.uk/community/networks-affiliates/bioimaginguk-network/uk-imaging-nodes/uk-bioimaging-user-access-fund.html> call. Future events
The event you attended last week is part of a series of four workshops sponsored by the Partnership Networking Fund<https://www.crick.ac.uk/research/research-partnerships/university-partnerships/partnership-networking-fund> and open to research students and staff of Imperial College, KCL and UCL. Our yearly Crick BioImage Analysis Symposium<https://www.crick.ac.uk/whats-on/crick-bioimage-analysis-symposium-2026> is happening at the Crick this November (23-24/11/26). The symposium will be followed by a workshop on using napari<https://napari.org/stable/index.html> for image analysis (25-26/11/26), you can find more information here<https://www.crick.ac.uk/whats-on/cbias-napari-workshop-2026>.

If you would like to discuss your image analysis with us after attending the workshop, you can book a follow-up meeting with me  here<https://outlook.office.com/bookwithme/user/d4b915488d774ba3bb17791e0c9e1b93@crick.ac.uk/meetingtype/NOe6dOCChEGIT7nj-TF70w2?bookingcode=96e94939-0dba-434a-943e-f0036387252c&anonymous&ismsaljsauthenabled&ep=mlink>.

Getting in touch with the Image Analysis team

**Advice on microglia quantification**

Hi team!

Thanks again for your time yesterday. You can find below a recap of what we discussed. If you think I've forgotten anything or have other questions, please don't hesitate to get in touch. 

Best wishes,
Stefania

---

  *
Some considerations on your images and current analysis:
     *
Working in 3D might be helpful for the analysis, as it might be easier to distinguish cells in the regions of the sample where they are packed close to each other.      *
The ImageJ tool you've tested so far might be limited in what it can achieve on your data, as it was developed to work on cells which were more spread out and not touching. However, the software wraps around other Fiji tools, which we could take a look at in the future if you think part of the morphological analysis they run can be helpful in your case.      *
Other tools worth a try are SNT<https://imagej.net/plugins/snt/>, which was developed for neurons, and GliaMorph<https://journals.biologists.com/dev/article/150/3/dev201008/286896/GliaMorph-a-modular-image-analysis-toolkit-to>. SNT has been used quite successfully by a few researchers at the Crick lately, so I would probably recommend starting there.      *
The variability of intensity you observe in different cells in the field of view might mean that traditional thresholding algorithms<https://neubias.github.io/training-resources/binarization/index.html> for segmentation fail on your cytoplasm channel. You could consider either pre-processing<https://neubias.github.io/training-resources/filter_convolution/index.html> the image before segmentation (e.g., smoothing with Gaussian blur, enhancing edges with Canny or Sobel filters, applying local contrast enhancement<https://imagej.net/plugins/clahe>) or testing alternative segmentation approaches.      *
One alternative approach is to use machine-learning segmentation algorithms. Ilastik<https://www.ilastik.org/> is an open-source software that you can use to achieve this. Its pixel classification workflow<https://www.ilastik.org/documentation/pixelclassification/pixelclassification> uses sparse training from the user to train a model to recognise the objects of interest, based not only on their intensity, but also on morphological and signal features. We have an upcoming training on ilastik<https://intranet.crick.ac.uk/seminar/image-analysis-machine-learning-based-image-analysis-ilastik-2026-08-28t080000> if you're interested, and their online documentation<https://www.ilastik.org/documentation/> is pretty good to get started.   *
The analysis pipeline aims to count microglia and measure their morphology. There are different approaches to this, but the following steps will likely be involved:      *
Count cells - using the nuclear channel for this is likely going to be easier, provided that only the microglia nuclei are stained. We discussed in the meeting the possibility of using a microglia-specific marker, which might help improve on the very packed DAPI signal you currently observe. Alternatively, you could look in 3D at the DAPI signal which overlaps with the microglia cytoplasm. The expectation is that microglia are mononuclear, so you should be able to "clean up" the DAPI signal in this way. Finally, you could use the microglia cytoplasm channel to count cells. This might be more challenging, especially in the busy regions where cells touch, but working in 3D could be helpful in discerning which processes belong to which cell.      *
Quantify microglia morphology - to achieve this, we need to make sure we can obtain a label mask of the green channel. This is an image where each cell is given a unique integer ID, so that it can be analysed as a separate object. Label masks are normally obtained by running connected components labelling<https://neubias.github.io/training-resources/connected_components/index.html> on binary masks, meaning that we first need to be successful in obtaining a binary mask from the green channel (see note about traditional thresholding vs. ilastik above). Due to the complex morphology of the microglia and their proximity, the easiest approach would be to work with a seeded watershed algorithm<https://imagej.net/plugins/marker-controlled-watershed>. This first locates "seeds", which are often represented by the centroid of the cell nucleus (provided a good enough nuclear staining can be obtained), and then expands them in all directions according to the signal on the channel of interest (cytoplasm in your case). While it's possible that some cell processes will not be split with perfect accuracy, this approach should allow you to distinguish individual cells. Implementation-wise, MorphoLibJ<https://imagej.net/plugins/marker-controlled-watershed> in Fiji or CellProfiler<https://cellprofiler.org/> can be used. Once a label mask is obtained, quantifying cell morphology should be relatively straightforward using a regionprops algorithm. This algorithm is implemented in most image analysis software (e.g., MorphoLibJ in Fiji), but you might want to look at neuron/glia specific tools to ensure the metrics of interest pertaining to processes are included.   *
There are different ways of working with CALM going forward, as detailed below:      *
Training: Get in touch when you have any questions! We'll have a chat similar to the one we had yesterday, in which we can advise on possible next steps and help with troubleshooting. This is currently free of charge.      *
Coaching: This is a new format we're testing. The idea is to set a specific timeframe and specific learning goals, which should revolve around learning a methodology rather than performing analysis on a specific dataset. The coaching programme is focused on skills and methods, not research outcomes. To use a paper analogy, we are coaching the Methods section, not the Results. The learning objectives specify the tools that the researcher will be able to use, the techniques they will understand, and the practices they will adopt. While they will be working on data relevant to their research project and receive help in interpreting outputs and troubleshooting the analysis, we can't guarantee that the analytical approaches will ultimately yield the expected biological results. On the other hand, the acquired methodological knowledge should equip the researcher with the relevant skills to tackle not only their current research question, but also to achieve a broader understanding of how to construct workflows for image analysis problems. You would meet regularly with your assigned coach; the sessions are meant for discussion of current progress, not live coding/analysis. CALM staff time would be charged according to current costs<https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1sMPvcBFGiFH3FI68NjZbcOOM439q6NJhBuGYSTCDTVU/edit?usp=sharing>; a cost estimate would be provided upon project agreement, but it's likely going to be around the cost of a medium project.      *
Project work - In this case, CALM staff would prepare the analysis pipeline or analyse a dataset for you. This is the only option in which we would be the ones working on your data directly, but this would still require your input and regular check-ins. CALM staff time would be charged according to current costs; a cost estimate and project plan would be provided upon project agreement.

**Request for a 1:1 consultation session**

Hi Quadri,

Thanks for your time yesterday. Please find below a recap of what we discussed. If I've forgotten anything or you have any additional questions, please get in touch! 

Best wishes,
Stefania

---

  *
The Brightness/Contrast menu<https://imagej.net/learn/brightness-and-contrast> in Fiji is for visualisation only; it doesn't change the histogram (i.e., the signal you acquired) unless you hit Apply (don't!). You can use the Auto button to improve the settings to "view" the images better.   *
Start with a scientific question and think of a metric that could quantify something which would help you answer it. For example, "I expect the treatment to increase nuclear size" could be assessed by quantifying the area of nuclei in control and treated conditions and comparing them. If that was indeed to show a difference, you can show two representative images, one for control and one for treatment, which can help convince your audience. But remember that we trust the numbers, not our eyes!   *
You can quantify signal by field of view. This involves looking at the mean grey value across the whole image for a given channel and comparing different experimental conditions. It can be achieved by selecting the mean grey value as an output (Analyse > Set measurements) and then quantifying with Analyse > Measure.   *
You can quantify signal in a specific region of interest. Usually, we go through a process of segmentation to obtain such regions, either on the channel we want to quantify or in a separate one. The simplest way to obtain segmentation is via thresholding<https://neubias.github.io/training-resources/binarization/index.html>, by picking an algorithm from the list in Image > Adjust > Threshold. This gives as output a binary mask, which highlights as positive the regions of the image for further quantification. We can use MorphoLibJ<https://imagej.net/plugins/morpholibj> (Plugins > MLJ > Analyse > Intensity measurements 2D/3D) to quantify another image in the positive regions of the binary mask.   *
Images can be pre-processed with filtering<https://neubias.github.io/training-resources/filter_convolution/index.html> (e.g., Gaussian blur) to improve signal-to-noise ratio and aid segmentation. Binary masks can also be cleaned or adjusted using morphological filters<https://neubias.github.io/training-resources/filter_morphological/index.html> or watershed<https://neubias.github.io/training-resources/watershed/index.html>.   *
You can obtain binary masks for different channels and create a joint mask using the image calculator tool<https://imagejdocu.list.lu/gui/process/image_calculator> (Process > Image Calculator, AND option). This will highlight regions of interest which were positive in both segmented channels.   *
You can quantify by region using label masks. These can be obtained by connected component labelling<https://neubias.github.io/training-resources/connected_components/index.html> (Plugins > MLJ > Binary masks > Connected components labelling) on any binary mask. In a label mask, each separate object is given a unique integer ID, allowing for individual queries both in terms of morphology (Plugins > MLJ > Analyse > Analyse regions) and signal intensity (Plugins > MLJ > Analyse > Intensity measurements 2D/3D).   *
Once you have a workflow, you can script a macro for automated batch processing in Fiji. You can follow the tutorial at this link<https://imagej.net/tutorials/batch-processing-with-ij-macro> to get started. Consider keeping your pipelines simple and targeted to a specific task to avoid confusion.   *
If you need assistance with running statistical analysis on the output data, you can contact the BABS team<https://intranet.crick.ac.uk/our-crick/bioinformatics-biostatistics/pages/statistics>, who provide stats support free of charge. 

________________________________

**helpdesk follow up**

Hi Yuexuan,

Thanks for stopping by the helpdesk this morning! Here's a recap of what we've discussed. If I have forgotten anything or you have further questions, please don't hesitate to get in touch. 

Best wishes,
Stefania

Stefania Marcotti

BioImage Analysis Trainer
Crick Image Analysis Group
Crick Advanced Light Microscopy (CALM) STP
The Francis Crick Institute
London, UK

  *
Regarding image acquisition, you might want to check with the CALM acquisition team whether something could be improved to increase the dynamic range and avoid possible bleed-through of the DAPI signal in the Golgi channel. As discussed earlier, it might not be bleed-through, but it might be worth checking to avoid quantifying signal that doesn't belong to the channel of interest! 

  *
For the analysis, you can either work in 2D or 3D. The pipeline would look basically the same, but the computational resources required increase when working with 3D data. Figuring out if your biological question requires the third dimensionality to be answered, or running a comparison might be a good idea at this stage! 

  *
We discussed running the analysis using Fiji. To do so, we first split the channels. We want to obtain two binary masks, one for the Golgi and one for your protein of interest. This is done by selecting a suitable thresholding<https://neubias.github.io/training-resources/binarization/index.html> algorithm from the list (Image > Adjust > Threshold); please note that the algorithm might be different between the two channels, but you'll want to keep the choice consistent across images. You might want to run some pre-processing steps, such as smoothing or filtering<https://neubias.github.io/training-resources/filter_convolution/index.html> to make the segmentation easier. You might also want to apply some morphological filters<https://neubias.github.io/training-resources/filter_morphological/index.html> to the binary masks for further cleaning. We can then use the image calculator (Process > Image Calculator) to find the pixels that are positive for both the Golgi and the protein of interest using the AND function between the two binary masks. This step will create a third binary mask, which is positive where both the Golgi and the protein of interest are present. You can now quantify the positive area in this new binary mask (Analyse > Measure; you might need to go to Image > Set Measurements and tick the Area checkbox) as a measure of colocalisation. Please note that, as discussed earlier, this measure alone doesn't tell you whether the two entities interact in any way! Just that they occupy a similar space.   *
Once you have a workflow you are happy with, you can automate the analysis over a folder of images by using macro scripting in Fiji. You can find here a tutorial<https://imagej.net/tutorials/batch-processing-with-ij-macro> for instructions on how to do so.

### Initial meeting – 27/7/26

Zoom with Sara. Email recap:

‌

Hi Rinako,

Thanks for your time today. Here’s a little recap of what we’ve just discussed.
I’m cc’ing Alessandro in case we need his LSM expertise.

Imaris issues
If you’re still struggling with setting up your pipeline in Imaris using your
current images, it’s worth contacting their support team directly
([eusupport_imaris@andor.com](mailto:eusupport_imaris@andor.com "‌")). They can also provide advice on the actual
pipeline itself, and are very responsive. Feel free to cc me in.

Decreased Z-steps
Using 4um instead of 10um Z-step will add over double the amount of slices to
your files, hence why it’s heavier and Imaris is struggling more than usual. For
the files you’ve already acquired, we can try removing some slices in FIJI to
reduce the size. It will make our life easier.

The bigger image analysis picture
If I understood correctly, the main aim of your analysis is to be able to
determine where in the lymph node your ‘pink’ cells are located. 

- I’d start with a more simple approach, and then add complexity as you go
  along. For instance, you could start with segmenting your ‘blue’ and ‘green’
  regions and quantifying how much ‘pink volume’ is covered in each of those
  regions.
- We can then dive a bit deeper into the dataset to find out whether there are
  subregions where these cells cluster

Analysis software
This can be done in open-source image analysis software. I’ll have a look at
different options with the raw files that you’ve just shared with me and get
back to you. But from what you’ve showed me during the meeting today, I’ll
probably go for:

- Ilastik [[https://www.ilastik.org/](https://www.ilastik.org/ "smartCard-inline")] – for the machine-learning aspect of the
  pipeline. It’s free to download and use, and has plenty of tutorials and
  documentation to help you get started. 
- Napari [[https://napari.org/stable/](https://napari.org/stable/ "smartCard-inline")] – a software made to visualise and
  interact multidimensional imaging datasets like yours. Getting started can be
  a bit challenging, but we can go through it together if needed when the time
  comes. 

Pink staining
If the pink staining is such a key part of the biological question you are
trying to answer, it’s worth seeing whether you can optimise the sample prep
steps. It will make the downstream analysis much clearer, and hence easier and
more robust. 

We’re a bit short of staff during the summer months, but I will try my best to
get back to you within the next couple of weeks. 

If you have any queries in the meantime, just reach out again.

Best wishes, 
Sara

**chat about quantification of CLEM data**

Hi MC,

Thanks again for your time yesterday! You can find below a recap of what we've discussed. Please let me know if I've forgotten anything or if you or your collaborators have any questions. 

Have a great weekend ahead,
Stefania

---

General considerations

  *
It might be worth running the analysis on separate tiles to limit the computational resources required. If the spatial information of where each tile is located proves to be important, it should be possible to use the stitching parameters from the raw data and apply them to the analysed images, without having to stitch everything multiple times.   *
If you want to work with stitched images or large fields of view, QuPath<https://qupath.github.io/> might be the best software, as it was developed for similar purposes. It's possible to implement the workflow discussed below in QuPath should you want to go down that route.   *
While the EM data might provide additional information on the "negative spaces" in the nuclei and the exact location of the nucleolus, I would start by analysing the LM data independently to keep things simple (and computationally cheap) to start with.   *
If your collaborators are planning to acquire more LM data and they are interested in quantifying distance to the nucleolus further, they might want to add a marker for it for easy identification (easier than segmenting EM data, that is).   *
BABS<https://intranet.crick.ac.uk/our-crick/bioinformatics-biostatistics> offers free statistical advice. I would chat to them to discuss how to represent the data, in particular how to group it by cell or field of view to run statistical analysis. You can read more about similar considerations in this paper<https://journals.biologists.com/jcs/article/139/10/jcs264367/371820/Practical-statistics-for-bioimage-analysis-a-guide>. 

Analysis pipeline (Fiji)

  *
First, segment the nuclei to obtain a label mask. This can be done by:      *
Pre-processing the DAPI channel with smoothing (e.g., Gaussian filter, Process > Filters > Gaussian Blur),      *
Choosing a thresholding<https://neubias.github.io/training-resources/binarization/index.html> algorithm (Image > Adjust > Threshold) for which each nucleus is highlighted as a homogeneous blob      *
Performing additional operations such as watershed<https://neubias.github.io/training-resources/watershed/index.html> (Process > Binary > Watershed) and morphological filtering<https://neubias.github.io/training-resources/filter_morphological/index.html> (Process > Binary > Erode/Dilate) if required to clean the binary mask obtained after thresholding. The aim is to separate each nucleus from its neighbours, if possible. I would advise against any manual correction and accept some minor inaccuracies as "good enough"<https://carpenter-singh-lab.broadinstitute.org/blog/when-to-say-good-enough>.      *
Creating a label mask<https://neubias.github.io/training-resources/connected_components/index.html> using MorphoLibJ<https://imagej.net/plugins/morpholibj> (Plugins > MorphoLibJ > Binary masks > Connected components labelling). This will assign an ID to each nucleus. MorphoLibJ has some built-in functions that can be used for cleaning binary and label masks, if needed (e.g., Plugins > MorphoLibJ > Label images > Remove border labels)   *
Next, segment the infection puncta to obtain a label mask. This requires similar steps to the ones listed above, but this time working on the other channel.   *
You will want to quantify the puncta label masks using MorphoLibJ to obtain coordinates and morphological parameters (Plugins > MorphoLibJ > Analyse> Analyse Regions) for further analysis   *
To study parent-child relationships, you can use the trick discussed in this post<https://forum.image.sc/t/is-there-a-way-to-count-the-number-of-small-objects-inside-large-objects-in-a-3d-image-by-morpholibj/8857/2> with MorphoLibJ. This allows you to calculate which puncta belong to each nucleus.   *
If you want to analyse the distance of puncta to negative chromatin spaces in the nuclei, you'll need to segment the nuclear channel again, this time without smoothing and choosing a different thresholding algorithm, which strictly selects high-signal regions. You'll obtain a binary mask, which you can use in conjunction with the coordinates of the puncta and the parent-child information to measure distances to negative spaces. This would be done mostly "numerically" without needing to perform additional operations on the images. 

How to work with CALM

  *
Training
Get in touch when you have any questions! We'll have a chat similar to the one we had yesterday, in which we can advise on possible next steps and help with troubleshooting. This is currently free of charge.   *
Coaching
This is a new format we're testing. The idea is to set a specific timeframe and specific learning goals, which should revolve around learning a methodology more than performing analysis on a specific dataset. The coaching programme is focused on skills and methods, not research outcomes. To use a paper analogy, we are coaching the Methods section, not the Results. The learning objectives specify the tools that the researcher will be able to use, the techniques they will understand, and the practices they will adopt. While they will be working on data relevant to their research project and receive help in interpreting outputs and troubleshooting the analysis, we can’t guarantee that the analytical approaches will ultimately yield the expected biological results. On the other hand, the acquired methodological knowledge should equip the researcher with the relevant skills to tackle not only their current research question, but also to achieve a broader understanding of how to construct workflows for image analysis problems. You would meet regularly with your assigned coach; the sessions are meant for discussion of current progress, not live coding/analysis. Joint coaching for you and your collaborator could be arranged if of interest. CALM staff time would be charged according to current costs<https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1sMPvcBFGiFH3FI68NjZbcOOM439q6NJhBuGYSTCDTVU/edit?usp=sharing>; a cost estimate and coaching plan would be provided upon project agreement.   *
Project work
In this case, CALM staff would prepare the analysis pipeline or analyse a dataset for you. This is the only option in which we would be the ones working on your data directly, but this would still require your input and regular check-ins. CALM staff time would be charged according to current costs; a cost estimate and project plan would be provided upon project agreement.

Hi Sanja, 

I'm sorry to hear you guys can't use Yuuki's pipeline.  I wasn't aware there were any issues, I have all the files backed up, and I'd have no problem trying to troubleshoot it for you when I return from holiday.

I'd follow up with Sara first.  I'm not sure who will be able to help you on such short notice, unfortunately, but I'll cc in the rest of the team.

Not seeing your data, I can throw a very very very random guess out that you can try something like CellPose to segment your cells in 3D. If that is sucessful, you can try to pass the segmentation maps to regionprops_table, a sci-kit image tool, which will allow you to measure the intensity of a second channel based on the map generated by the first channel.  

Basically -->

Segment Cells using CellPose --> use regionprops_table to find intensity of probe channel in segmented cells 

The huge caveat, other than I've not seen your data, is that you don't want to only segment on HuC/D if you are looking for HuC/D positive cells in a population of many cells. 

Again, I'd try to get in touch with Sara first, then anyone else in Calm that can maybe help you, but with slightly tempered expectations, as a lot of us are on holiday these weeks! Sorry!

## 1st meeting – 20/7/26

Email recap:

Hi Leigh,

Thanks for sending over such neat and organised info on the project! As mentioned in our meeting yesterday, here is a recap on what we discussed:

**IHC pipelines**

The analyses that you need done in these set of images are essentially what we did during the course, so you can find those scripts in the course materials.

- Granuloma annotation (H&E): a pixel classifier should give you information to extract granuloma area and count, exactly like in the 1st part of the course workflow. 
- ZN bacteria counting: you can try positive cell detection with QuPath’s inbuilt algorithm. Playing with the main parameters should give you a fairly decent segmentation. If it’s over segmenting them because of their rod-shape, we can try using pre-trained deep learning models (like Instanseg, Cellpose, or Stardist). Maybe someone has trained a model on similar data and uploaded it onto [BioImage Model Zoo](https://bioimage.io/#/models "‌"). 
- p24 quantification: once you have the granuloma annotations, you can run another positive cell detection function and extract %area covered, or just extract the mean OD of the p24 stain in the granuloma annotations vs whole-node.

Remember to apply colour deconvolution to your images before any analysis, so you can improve the “purity” of the stains and improve how well the downstream analysis performs. For it, select a representative region of the image with background, parenchyma, and clear stain of interest. 

**Phenocycler-fusion multiplex pipeline**

      We can use QuPath to make a full pipeline for the simpler proximity questions you are asking (e.g., macrophage distance to granuloma core) . You can extract distance-to-annotation measurements or density maps directly in the software. 

      However, for the more complex spatial analysis, we can create the first part of the pipeline in QuPath (import images > tissue and granuloma annotation > cell segmentation > phenotyping, feature measurement). We can then extract the per-cell expression matrices (cells x markers) to do downstream analysis in dedicated Python/R packages. This is where **BABS** come in. 

      Once you chat to Cami tomorrow, I can reach out to the BABS team to get some assistance and cc you all in. 

**Lymphoma controls**

Definitely use these to check background and non-specific staining per marker. It’ll help you set the gating thresholds and train classifiers!

Speak soon, 

Sara

## 1st meeting – 21/7/26

Email recap:

Hi Orla, 

Thank you for your time today. As mentioned, here’s a recap of what we discussed with a few useful links – beware, long email incoming.

**QuPath on OnDemand**

You can absolutely work locally, but making the most of our High Performance Computing (HPC) cluster to access more powerful computers will speed up your analysis, especially with big images like whole slide images.

If you’ve already accessed OnDemand before, you can just request a session and follow [these instructiions](https://franciscrickinstitute.github.io/Image-Analysis-Group/software_instructions/QuPath/ "‌") to access QuPath v0.7 – no need for installation!

**Pixel Classifier issue: AutoFL batch-to-batch variability** 

Plan A: try a few different features

- You are currently using just the absolute AutoFL intensity to train the classifier, which makes your results _very_ susceptible to variability, even if you are using annotations from different images.
- Try adding features to capture relative textures and patterns, rather than absolute brightness. 
  - Start with _Lapplacian of Gaussian_ and _Structure tensor coherence_ with a few different scales. These highlight edges, which might reveal patterns to discern your region of interest in a much more robust way.

![Screenshot 2026-07-21 at 13.14.03.png](cid:57A60B09-2BC3-46CD-AA52-DA224A69CBCB)

- You can see the effect of each of the features by clicking on the dropdown menu just under the pixel classifier viewer, where it says _Show classification_. 
- Still use different batches to train and test it.
- A very nice way to see how much each feature “matters” for the classifier if using the _Random trees_ type, is by clicking “Edit” and selecting “Calculate variable importance”. 
  - Once you apply the classifier, you can go to the log and see which features matter most for its final decision (higher numbers = higher importance):

      1:

![Screenshot 2026-07-21 at 13.20.17.png](cid:0D865460-0A3F-462E-852B-CB3FDADF6ACB)

      2:

![Screenshot 2026-07-21 at 13.22.36.png](cid:1DD1111C-0314-4849-BCF0-DE9B4CE19C1D)

      3:

![Screenshot 2026-07-21 at 13.24.23.png](cid:F8C94E5F-E8E1-42E6-B36D-61D165D193C7)

If you do still get very stuck, let me know and I can have a look too.

Plan B: per-image normalisation before classification

- We can try adding a pre-processing step before you train the classifier to normalise the AutoFL channel to its own distribution.
- NOTE – QuPath does have a “local normalisation” option that applies a local background subtraction and normalisation, but the developers urge people to avoid using it. We’re better off trying a global normalisation approach. 
- It can’t be done in the QuPath GUI, but there seem to be ways of doing this through a Groovy script (more info [here](https://qupath.github.io/javadoc/docs/qupath/opencv/ops/ImageOps.Normalize.html "‌")). 

**Hippocampus detection automation**

The only way to do this in an automated manner, unless you have a specific hippocampal fluorescent marker, is by aligning your images to an atlas.

- The obvious choice is using FIJI’s [ABBA](https://abba-documentation.readthedocs.io/en/v0.11.0/tutorial/4_qupath_analysis.html "‌") which can interact nicely with QuPath.
- However, if you’ve tried it before and it was giving you a big headache to adapt to your sagittal slices, and manual ROI detection isn’t much of a hassle, we can stick to that. 
- We can always revisit this approach if we reach a dead end with the pixel classifier. 

If you encounter any issues or have any questions in the meantime, feel free to reach out again. 

Best of luck!

Sara

Hi Richard,

Happy to help.

If I understand correctly, the first step is to register/align the H&E with
coreponding CosMx run (using the IF image?) and then segment structures in the

answer. It may be possible to train a pixel classifier or there’s quite possibly
a suitable pre-trained deep learning model out there somewhere (there seems to
be one for almost everything these days). I assume the lab who generated the
data usually do this sort of thing manually?

‌

Dave.

data.text:
**CALM helpdesk**

Hi Clare,

Sorry for the delay in getting back to you, I've asked Dave as well whether he had any further ideas on how to tackle your query. 

We agree overall with the approach you've taken so far: the Fiji plugin you are using<https://github.com/Biomedical-Imaging-Group/EDF-Extended-Depth-of-Field> might not be the most up to date, but it's from a trustworthy source and does what you need. Should it fail at some point in the future, it should be relatively straightforward to replicate the algorithm in Python if necessary (we can assist in case). 

We've also discussed some alternative approaches you might want to explore: 

  *
Z-projection: while a relatively crude approach, projecting the two images in the Stack in Z (such as with a max projection) achieves quite a decent sharpened output   *
Fourier space: calculating the Fourier transforms (vertical and horizontal components) of the image and applying a high-pass filter will enhance the edges, practically achieving sharpening of the image. You can read more here<https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/computer-vision/fast-fourier-transform-in-image-processing/>. It should be possible to implement this in Fiji<https://imagejdocu.list.lu/gui/process/fft>.   *
PSF: if it is possible to acquire a 3D stack with your imaging method, you might want to consider imaging some beads instead of your current test sample. This would allow you to then reconstruct an experimental point spread function (PSF) equivalent with software such as Huygens<https://svi.nl/Huygens-Software>, and you can then deconvolve the images acquired on experimental samples with the calculated PSF. 

I hope this helps! If you require further assistance in implementing any of the mentioned alternatives, or would like to discuss any additional details, please get in touch. We can organise a meeting if necessary. 

Best wishes,
Stefania

Hi Anson,

 

Sorry, didn’t realise you had already done some quantification. Ok, probably
worth arranging a chat about this, but I have a few more questions, just to
provide me with a little more context:

 * How much image data do you already have?
    * Is it on NEMO or elsewhere (I assume the latter if acquired at UCL)?
    * And how much more (if any) do you plan to acquire?

 * Will you just have these two conditions or will there be others?
 * Your images are in 3D – are you performing the analysis in 3D or in 2D?
    * If 2D, are you projecting the data to two dimensions or selecting a
      particular plane in the stack?

 * What have you been using to do the quantification up to this point?
    * Do you want to stick with that, or have you found it limiting and want to
      try something else?

 

On another important note, the p values on your plots are suspiciously small
(and probably not necessary given your results are clear without them) – I
recommend discussing with someone in the BioStatistics team in BABS.

 

My diary is a bit full at the moment, but I’m pretty free on Friday the 24th for
a chat?

card.desc:
Here is the information in preparation for the meeting.

Representative images can be found on OMERO under OK\_20x\_20260303. It is a dataset with 5 channels of some sagittal brain slices.

**What is the biological question you are trying to answer?**
Our lab is interested in autoimmune psychosis. As part of our clinical studies, we receive patient serum and CSF samples, which we screen for autoantibodies using a range of methods. One of our aims is to identify patterns in antibody binding across different patient groups and determine whether there are distinct antibody profiles associated with specific clinical cases.

**Briefly describe the samples you are imaging/have imaged.**
The images are from a tissue-based assay using mouse brain sections. Patient serum or CSF is used as the primary antibody source, followed by immunostaining and whole-slide scanning. We have been sending the slides to Donald for scanning.

**What measurement(s) would you like to get out of your analysis?**
We quantify the mean fluorescence intensity (MFI) in specific brain regions. Previously, this has been done by manually drawing ROIs in QuPath and extracting the MFI values. We are now trying to automate this process.

**With what microscope did you acquire your images? Was it with someone from the CALM STP?**
The images were acquired by Donald through the CALM STP as whole-slide scans.

**How many images do you have? Are you planning to acquire more?**
Around 200 available training images from different scanning session.

**What channel(s) do you have in the shared images? Conditions/Controls?**
The images contain the immunofluorescence channel used to detect patient antibody binding, along with the nuclear stain. The dataset includes both patient samples and control samples.

**Is there any reference paper you are following for the analysis?**
No specific analysis paper. Our current workflow has been developed in-house.

To give some additional context, I have already trained a QuPath pixel classifier that can accurately distinguish the hippocampus and surrounding regions. We found that analysing this area alone is sufficient to discriminate between cases and controls, and the MFI values extracted using the classifier correlate strongly with those obtained using manually drawn ROIs.

One problem I have had with the classifier is that both DAPI and AutoFL are necessary for distinguishing regions, but the AutoFL can be very variable between scanning sessions, how to overcome this?

The remaining challenge is that the classifier currently requires me to manually draw a polygon around the hippocampus before running the analysis. We were wondering whether QuPath has a way to automatically identify or generate this polygon so that the entire workflow could be fully automated.

we observe is due to direct effects of TDP-43 LoF on the Golgi or a more

networks; as such we are trying to quantify whether either network is perturbed.

appropriate analyses, such branching analyses.

look at actin and tubulin. We’ve been using the LSM980 over at UCL for our
imaging.

Whatever method you select, make sure to check whether you agree with the results by looking back at the images after you categorised each object.

**Trajectory analysis**

Hi Julia,

Sorry for the delay in getting back to you!

I haven't managed to have a chat with Matt yet to enquire about the strategy he had in mind; I'll try again later today. 

I was recently contacted by Haonan in your lab, who told me he was working on an algorithm to analyse the same dataset, and it sounded like he was quite advanced in their approach for tracking single particles. Have you checked with them recently? 

A simple approach in Fiji could be to subtract the first frame from the last frame of your videos (Process> Image Calculator (subtract)) and measure the mean gray value of the output image (Analyze> Measure, you'll have to make sure "mean gray value" is selected in Analyze> Set Measurements). This can be used as a proxy for movement, as the resulting image will contain a higher signal the more the beads have moved. 

Cheers,
Stefania

**image analysis - meeting notes**

Hi Anais,

Thanks for your time yesterday. Please find below a recap of what we've discussed, let me know if you think I've forgotten anything! 

Best wishes,
Stefania

---

  *
Importing files in Fiji: please use Bio-Formats<https://www.openmicroscopy.org/bio-formats/> (File> Import> Bio-Formats) to open your raw files. This ensures that the metadata is read correctly.   *
You can run Fiji on OnDemand. You can find more information about OnDemand on the HPC wiki<https://wiki.thecrick.org/display/HPCuserwiki/OnDemand>, and you can find instructions on how to install and run Fiji on OnDemand at this link<https://github.com/FrancisCrickInstitute/Image-Analysis-Group/tree/master/software_instructions/Fiji>.   *
You can take a look at this tutorial<https://imagej.net/tutorials/batch-processing-with-ij-macro> if you're interested in automating the analysis using Fiji macros.   *
To analyse the green/red puncta in your images, we discussed the following pipeline:      *
Label the nuclei
     *
Label the puncta on both green and red channels
     *
Measure the puncta per nuclei
  *
To label any structure we follow these steps:
     *
(optional) pre-process the image using filters. We looked at Gaussian blur<https://neubias.github.io/training-resources/filter_convolution/index.html> (Process> Filters> Gaussian Blur) for the DAPI channel. This aims at reducing the noise in the image to improve segmentation      *
Semantic segmentation. We are splitting the image histogram into two parts by using an algorithm to locate a threshold<https://neubias.github.io/training-resources/binarization/index.html>. The resulting image is called a binary mask, and it's going to contain only two values, 0 for background and 255 for foreground. Choose an algorithm from the list (Image> Adjust> Threshold) that selects the regions of the image you want to select.      *
(optional) post-process the binary masks. You can use morphological filters<https://neubias.github.io/training-resources/filter_morphological/index.html> to clean the binary masks (Process> Binary)      *
Instance segmentation. We can assign IDs to each object to analyse them separately. To do this, we exploit a plugin, MorphoLibJ<https://imagej.net/plugins/morpholibj>, which allows us to create a label mask<https://neubias.github.io/training-resources/connected_components/> from the binary mask using connected component labelling (Plugins> MorphoLibJ> Binary Images> Connected Component Labeling).      *
(optional) post-process the label masks. MorphoLibJ has a few tools to clean labels based on area (Plugins> MorphoLibJ> Label Images> Label size filtering) and to clear the image border (Plugins> MorphoLibJ> Label Images> Remove Border Labels)   *
To measure the size and shape of puncta, we can use Plugins> MorphoLibJ> Analyze> Analyze Regions 3D. This also allows to obtain object centroid, which you'll need to compute any distances between puncta. All output from MorphoLibJ can be exported as csv for further analysis.   *
To measure whether puncta belong to the nuclei, we can use the approach detailed in this blog post<https://forum.image.sc/t/is-there-a-way-to-count-the-number-of-small-objects-inside-large-objects-in-a-3d-image-by-morpholibj/8857/2>, with Plugins> MorphoLibJ> Analyze> Intensity Measurements 2D/3D.   *
You can get assistance with statistics from the wonderful people in the BABS team<https://intranet.crick.ac.uk/our-crick/bioinformatics-biostatistics>.   *
We have an upcoming Fiji workshop<https://intranet.crick.ac.uk/seminar/image-analysis-introduction-fiji-image-analysis-2026-07-31t083000> on July 31st, if you're interested.
